extracted.intended_audience: citizens and voters of New York; readers considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for structuring a representative legislative body (size, apportionment, knowledge, checks) as argued in The Federalist Papers (Nos. LV–LVIII). Focuses on what makes the House of Representatives safe and competent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common measure for representation and taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As the accuracy of the census to be obtained by the Congress will necessarily depend, in a considerable degree on the disposition, if not on the co-operation, of the States... By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests, which will control and balance each other, and produce the requisite impartiality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same rule to determine both representation and taxation so that states have opposing incentives (to swell population for representation vs reduce it for taxation), promoting impartiality and accurate returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate total number of representatives (balance deliberation and avoid mob)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A certain number at least seems to be necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion, and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes; as, on the other hand, the number ought at most to be kept within a certain limit, in order to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a number large enough to permit deliberation and prevent collusion, but not so large as to produce disorder or render debate ineffective. The paper gives concrete early-US figures (initially sixty‑five; census-based increases to about one per 30,000) as illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for periodic augmentation and apportionment (census every ten years)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Within every successive period of ten years the census is to be renewed, and augmentations may continue to be made under the above limitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed mechanisms (decennial censuses and periodic reapportionment) to allow the representative body to scale with population, subject to limits (e.g., not to exceed one representative per 30,000 inhabitants and each state at least one representative). This prevents permanent underrepresentation as population grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fewer representatives permissible when powers are limited and state legislatures provide control
rubrics_metrics.description: 'For the same reason that the limited powers of the Congress, and the control of the State legislatures, justify less frequent elections than the public safety might otherwise require, the members of the Congress need be less numerous than if they possessed the whole power of legislation... '
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of federal authority and the existence of state-level checks justify a smaller federal chamber than would be necessary for a body with plenary power; institutional context affects appropriate size and election frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives need knowledge only of matters within the purview of federal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is a sound and important principle that the representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents. But this principle can extend no further than to those circumstances and interests to which the authority and care of the representative relate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representatives by their familiarity with subjects they must legislate on (commerce, taxation, militia). Detailed knowledge of minutiae unrelated to federal powers is not necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws and state legislatures as primary sources of local information
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The laws of the State, framed by representatives from every part of it, will be almost of themselves a sufficient guide... The federal councils will derive great advantage from another circumstance. The representatives of each State will... probably in all cases have been members, and may even at the very time be members, of the State legislature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the federal legislative process to rely on compilations of state legislation and the experience of state legislators; a few well-informed delegates can convey local knowledge into federal deliberations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative ratio of one per thirty thousand inhabitants is adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Allowing to this case the weight which is due to it, and comparing it with that of the House of Representatives as above explained it seems to give the fullest assurance, that a representative for every THIRTY THOUSAND INHABITANTS will render the latter both a safe and competent guardian of the interests which will be confided to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical comparisons (e.g., British House of Commons representation) and projected population growth to justify target representative-to-population ratios; the paper endorses ~1:30,000 as a defensible standard for the proposed Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent elections as a principal restraint on corruption and ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hence, in the fourth place, the House of Representatives is so constituted as to support in the members an habitual recollection of their dependence on the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short terms and regular elections should be used as a structural check that keeps representatives accountable and discourages schemes that would elevate a few at the expense of the many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility to accept certain civil offices during term to prevent bribery
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The members of the Congress are rendered ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or of which the emoluments may be increased, during the term of their election.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit sitting legislators from being appointed to newly created or enhanced-emolument offices during their term to remove a channel for purchasing legislative compliance; this reduces opportunities for executive corruption via patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws should bind lawmakers as well as the people (self‑applicability of statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'They can make no law which will not have its full operation on themselves and their friends, as well as on the great mass of the society.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design legislation so its effects also apply to legislators and their close circles where appropriate; the shared impact of laws is a bond linking rulers to the governed and discourages self‑serving special legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger electorates tend to produce fitter representatives and resist corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reason, on the contrary, assures us, that as in so great a number a fit representative would be most likely to be found, so the choice would be less likely to be diverted from him by the intrigues of the ambitious or the bribes of the rich.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, have electoral districts with substantially larger electorates (thousands rather than hundreds) to (a) increase chance of selecting qualified candidates and (b) reduce vulnerability to manipulation by ambitious actors or monetary influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing political design solely on arithmetic ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nothing can be more fallacious than to found our political calculations on arithmetical principles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement numerical rules (ratios, quotas) with qualitative judgment about civic character, institutional context, and administrative practicability; size and proportions require both numerical and contextual reasoning rather than pure calculation.
